one_liner: Pure-Go static string-to-index table (CHD-style minimal perfect hash); author's 2021 benchmark shows 27% faster lookups than map[string]uint32.
what_it_does: Builds an immutable lookup table from a fixed []string. Lookup(s) returns the key's index in that slice plus a found flag, and values live in a parallel slice indexed by that result. The whole API is Build(keys []string) *Table and (*Table).Lookup(string) (uint32, bool). There is no insert, delete, iteration, generics or serialization, so replacing a read-only map[string]T takes a small refactor.
how_it_is_fast: Build hashes keys with Murmur3 (seed 0) into about n/4 buckets and sorts the buckets largest-first. For each bucket it searches for a Murmur3 seed that sends all of the bucket's keys to free slots in a power-of-two array. This is the hash-and-displace step of CHD (Belazzougui, Botelho, Dietzfelbinger, ESA 2009) without the compress step. A Lookup is two seeded Murmur3 hashes, two uint32 array reads and one string compare against the stored key, with no probing and no collision chains. The 32-bit Murmur3 is hand-written and reads 4-byte blocks directly from the string bytes via unsafe.
when_to_use: Read-heavy Go code with a fixed set of string keys known at startup (keywords, routes, dictionary words, enum names), where lookup latency matters and rebuilds are rare.
Short keys such as dictionary words: all published wins are on word lists (about 102k and 348k words), and the key is hashed twice per lookup.
Lookups that include absent keys: Lookup compares against the stored key, so a non-member returns ok=false instead of a bogus index.
When you want a zero-dependency file to vendor: 165 lines of non-test Go in two files, MIT-licensed.
Toolchains older than Go 1.24, where the built-in map was the pre-Swiss-table design that every published mph benchmark was run against.
when_not_to_use: Keys that change at runtime. The Table is immutable, so any insert or delete means a full rebuild. The README gives 18 ms for 102k words on an i7-8700K, and the PR #4 benchstat shows 32.7 MB and 302k allocations per Build for about 348k words.

Go 1.24 or later without re-benchmarking. Go 1.24 moved the built-in map to Swiss Tables, which the Go blog says are up to 60% faster on map microbenchmarks. The README's own margin already shrank from 'almost twice as fast' (2016) to 28% (2018) and then 27% (2021).
Long keys. Each Lookup runs a scalar 32-bit Murmur3 over the whole key twice. Issue #3 measured that hash at 16.3 ns for 50 bytes and 202 ns for 500 bytes on a Xeon.

Tight memory budgets or very large key sets. Seeds and slots are uncompressed uint32 arrays (roughly 5-10 bytes per key after power-of-two rounding), and the table also keeps the full keys slice. That is far above the 2-3 bits/key of compact MPHFs.
Non-string keys, or tables you want to persist. Only string keys are supported, and with no serialization the table is rebuilt at every process start.

integration.min_toolchain: go.mod declares go 1.17; no generics are used
integration.platforms: any Go target in principle; all published results are amd64 (i7-8700K, Skylake laptop, Xeon); the hash does native-endian, possibly unaligned uint32 loads through unsafe
integration.thread_safety: The Table is documented as immutable and Lookup only reads, so concurrent Lookups are safe by construction. Concurrency is not stated explicitly.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — it replaces only a read-only map[string]uint32-style index. Values must move to a parallel slice, and there is no insert, delete, range or len.

gotchas: Duplicate keys make Build loop forever. Two identical keys collide under every seed, and the seed search has no retry limit and no error return.
Build on an empty slice returns a Table whose Lookup panics with index out of range, because it always reads keys[n] and the slice is empty.
The Table keeps a reference to the caller's keys slice, not a copy. Modifying that slice after Build silently breaks lookups.

murmur.go uses the deprecated reflect.SliceHeader/StringHeader to load native-endian uint32 words. Its test vectors are the standard little-endian Murmur3 values, and the repo has no CI, so big-endian and strict-alignment targets are untested.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: The other Go entry, dgryski/go-mph, uses one metro hash per query and depends on go-metro, and because it stores no keys an absent key returns an arbitrary index. Pick cespare/mph over it when you need built-in membership checks and zero dependencies. Pick it over C++/Rust MPHFs such as PTHash or PtrHash (2-3 bits/key, scaling to billions of keys) only in pure-Go code with modest key counts where storing the keys is acceptable.
verified_claims_summary: The README's go test -bench run on an Intel i7-8700K (2021; Go toolchain not stated, so the old pre-Swiss-table map) looked up each word of a ~102k-entry /usr/share/dict/words in turn: Table.Lookup took 29.99 ns/op and map[string]uint32 took 40.92 ns/op, 27% less time for mph. A third-party run in issue #3 (2022, Xeon 2.80GHz, 348,454 words) measured 35.4 vs 67.8 ns/op, and nobody has published a run on Go 1.24 or later.
status_note: Abandoned: the last commit and the only tag (v0.1.0) date from 2021-09-01, and a 2022 PR (#4) that switches to xxh3 for ~23% faster lookups is still unmerged. The code is MIT-licensed and 165 lines, so it is easy to vendor and patch.
